newsitem.title: UK: Mark gets German lip service but analysts want more.
newsitem.headline: Mark gets German lip service but analysts want more.

text.p: German officials are going to have to do a little bit more than drop the odd remark to take the mark out of the doldrums, analysts said on Friday.
"The market is unimpressed with verbal intervention now, to be honest, we've heard so much," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
"Why should the market take them seriously until they show themselves to have a little bit more behind them?"
The mark dropped to six-year lows against the dollar early this week, partly on a belief Europe's planned single currency may be weaker than the mark if and when it is launched in 1999.
As the dollar scraped the 1.80-mark level, having risen steadily from around 1.55 at the start of the year, the market became awash with official German statements.

On Tuesday, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the mark's weakness, notably against a strong dollar and British pound, was part of a market "overreaction". He added Germany was in contact with Group of Seven partners.
Wednesday saw German government spokesman Peter Haussmann say there was no reason to "dramatise" recent developments on the forex markets.
On Thursday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said forex developments were being watched "very carefully".
Finally, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday said a somewhat stronger dollar against the mark was not an "earth-shaking" matter.
While the comments injected sufficient nerves about the possibility of intervention to keep a lid on dollar/mark at 1.80, they did not reverse mark losses.
"The market is not going to move (in favour of the mark) until it really does fear intervention," said Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Banque Paribas in London.
Otherwise the market would need a catalyst such as signs of an EMU delay, much faster growth in Europe, a rise in German interest rates, or clear signs of import-driven inflation.

Parsons said key signals could come from the mark's trade-weighted index. The index is measured against a basket of 20 other currencies, so mark declines could no longer be explained away as a dollar or sterling story, for example, he said.
The index, fixed by the Bank of England, stands at 102.1 percent, and has fallen 4.6 percent so far this year. The year's low was on Tuesday when it fell to 101.8 percent.
"If it (the mark) drops below 100 (percent) on the trade-weighted index it slips from a first division currency to the second division," Parsons said.
The base year for the index is 1990 so it would mean the mark, broadly speaking, would be weaker than seven years ago.

While German officials have said dollar and sterling strength reflected the state of their economies, Parsons said they had not applied the same logic to mark weakness. "It was the one thing they couldn't say."
Fiscally, Germany has its hands tied by commitments to rein in the budget deficit. On the monetary side, a rise in interest rates would fly in the face of attempts to bolster the economy.
"They're a bit stuck," said Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC Markets.
Kohl's "earth-shaking" comment was far too relaxed, the cabinet statements were disappointing relative to market expectations, and the Bundesbank has failed to put its foot down, he said.
"The rhetoric has not been terribly convincing and doesn't look like it will be backed up by any significant action."
The market feeling of a broad-based EMU had not been fully discounted by the market and, as a result, the mark may have further to fall in the short term, King said.
Rayner at SGST said perhaps the only thing that would prompt a market reaction would be a G7 statement. "One-sided" German statements would do little to reverse the trade, he said.
Although inflationary pressure on the import side was some way off, Rayner said the mark could continue to slide from these levels indefinitely.
"They're not going to be overly concerned that the mark has been weak, but you can't let it go forever."
